title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
description:
# Peak Index in a Mountain Array

An array `arr` is a **mountain array** when it strictly increases up to one peak and then strictly decreases after that peak.

More formally, there is an index `i` with `0 < i < arr.length - 1` such that:

* `arr[0] < arr[1] < ... < arr[i - 1] < arr[i]`
* `arr[i] > arr[i + 1] > ... > arr[arr.length - 1]`

Given a mountain array `arr`, return the peak index `i`.

Use `O(log(arr.length))` time.

## Example 1

**Input:** arr = [0,1,0]

**Output:** 1

## Example 2

**Input:** arr = [0,2,1,0]

**Output:** 1

## Example 3

**Input:** arr = [0,10,5,2]

**Output:** 1

## Constraints

* `3 <= arr.length <= 100000`
* `0 <= arr[i] <= 1000000`
* `arr` is guaranteed to be a mountain array.

solutions.name: Half-Open Slope Binary Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

Binary search the remaining interval using the local slope between `arr[mid]` and `arr[mid + 1]`. If the slope is rising, the peak must be to the right of `mid`; otherwise `mid` is either the peak or on the falling side, so keep the left half including `mid`.

## Key Insight

In a valid mountain array, the predicate `arr[i] > arr[i + 1]` becomes true exactly when we reach the peak or move past it. That monotonic change lets us discard half of the array.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Closed Interval with Peak Predicate
solutions.description:
## Approach

Search only possible peak indices, from `1` to `arr.length - 2`. At each midpoint, check whether it is greater than both neighbors. If the right neighbor is larger, the midpoint is still on the rising side; otherwise it is on the falling side.

## Key Insight

The peak is the only index that is greater than both neighbors. Neighbor checks make the target condition explicit, while the slope still tells us which half can contain the peak.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Ternary Search on a Unimodal Array
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat the mountain as a discrete unimodal function. Compare two interior points: when `arr[mid1] < arr[mid2]`, the peak is not to the left of `mid1`; otherwise it is not to the right of `mid2`. Once a tiny interval remains, scan only those few candidates.

## Key Insight

Binary search uses adjacent slope; ternary search uses the single-peak shape directly. Each iteration removes a constant fraction of the remaining interval, so the search remains logarithmic.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Recursive Slope Binary Search
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the same slope rule recursively. A rising midpoint sends the search to `[mid + 1, right]`; a falling midpoint keeps `mid` and searches `[left, mid]`. The base case returns the only remaining index.

## Key Insight

The recursive version exposes the invariant clearly: every recursive range still contains the peak. We never discard `mid` when the slope is falling, because `mid` itself may be the peak.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(log n)
- Space Complexity: O(log n)
